evidence.claim: Prairie hills above a river valley carved by glacial meltwater
evidence.quote: Surging glacial meltwaters carved deep into soft glacial drift to form the middle Little Sioux River valley. Today, steep, unplowed prairie-cloaked hills flank this meandering river

evidence.claim: The Glacial Trail Scenic Byway makes a paved, 36-mile loop through northwest Iowa.
evidence.quote: TRAIL USES: Driving LENGTH: 36 miles SURFACE: Paved

evidence.claim: It crosses the corners of O'Brien, Clay, Buena Vista and Cherokee counties through Peterson and Linn Grove.
evidence.quote: The Byway is a 36-mile loop drive that takes some surprising turns through O'Brien, Clay, Buena Vista and Cherokee counties and the rural towns of Peterson and Linn Grove.

evidence.claim: Steep hills carrying unplowed prairie flank the winding Little Sioux River, above valley land divided between woods and farms. Golden Hills RC&D, which coordinates the byway, identifies its natural, scenic, archaeological and historic qualities as the focus of the corridor.
evidence.quote: Today, steep, unplowed prairie-cloaked hills flank this meandering river and forested and farmed valley.

evidence.claim: Glacial meltwater cut the middle Little Sioux valley deep into soft deposits left by ice.
evidence.quote: Surging glacial meltwaters carved deep into soft glacial drift to form the middle Little Sioux River valley.

evidence.claim: Later park building added another layer to this landscape. At Wanata, south of Peterson, Dr. E.W. Spaulding helped acquire land for a park dedicated in 1934. Civilian Conservation Corps Company 778 built a stone shelter on a hillside descending toward the river.
evidence.quote: Dr. E.W. Spaulding from Peterson was instrumental in acquiring the property for the park, which was dedicated in 1934. Civilian Conservation Corps Company 778 built the shelter on the slope of a hill that descends to the Little Sioux River.

evidence.claim: Start in Peterson, where the fort's blockhouse remains near Second and Park, and include the shelter south of town as a separate excursion.
evidence.quote: The blockhouse from this fort still stands near its original location at the corner of Second and Park.

evidence.claim: Continue through the loop to Linn Grove, also near the Little Sioux River. The Prairie Heritage Center outside Peterson adds geological context and a restored prairie to the circuit.
evidence.quote: Linn Grove is situated near the Little Sioux River.

evidence.claim: through northwest Iowa
evidence.quote: its 36-mile loop in northwest Iowa.

evidence.claim: Golden Hills RC&D, which coordinates the byway
evidence.quote: The Glacial Trail Scenic Byway is coordinated with the help of an advisory council and Project Coordinator Seth Brooks at Golden Hills RC&D

evidence.claim: identifies its natural, scenic, archaeological and historic qualities as the focus of the corridor
evidence.quote: market the intrinsic natural, scenic, archaeological, and historic qualities of the byway

evidence.claim: south of Peterson
evidence.quote: Wanata State Park Picnic Shelter is a historic building located south of Peterson, Iowa, United States.

evidence.claim: The Prairie Heritage Center outside Peterson adds geological context and a restored prairie to the circuit.
evidence.quote: The Prairie Heritage Center near Peterson provides information about the geology and natural history of the area. Learn about glacial remnants, including kames and kettles, glacial till, hanging valleys and catsteps, all in one place. View a restored prairie

evidence.claim: Unplowed prairie covers steep hills above the wooded and farmed Little Sioux valley.
evidence.quote: steep, unplowed prairie-cloaked hills flank this meandering river and forested and farmed valley.

evidence.claim: Peterson's blockhouse stands near its original site at Second and Park. Settlers built the fort in 1862 because they anticipated Dakota attacks during the Dakota War. The fort was never attacked.
evidence.quote: In 1862, a fort was built in Peterson by settlers to defend against anticipated Dakota attacks during the Dakota War, though the fort was never attacked. The blockhouse from this fort still stands near its original location at the corner of Second and Park.

evidence.claim: The town's later development followed another transport connection: Peterson was platted in 1881 when the railroad arrived. The surviving blockhouse therefore predates that town plan.
evidence.quote: Peterson was platted in 1881 when the railroad was extended to that point.

evidence.claim: The blockhouse remains near its original location at Second and Park.
evidence.quote: The blockhouse from this fort still stands near its original location at the corner of Second and Park.

evidence.claim: Stone walls and timber supports meet on the hillside above the Little Sioux River at Wanata's picnic shelter.
evidence.quote: Civilian Conservation Corps Company 778 built the shelter on the slope of a hill that descends to the Little Sioux River.

evidence.claim: Dr. E.W. Spaulding of Peterson helped secure the park property, dedicated in 1934, and Civilian Conservation Corps Company 778 built the shelter.
evidence.quote: Dr. E.W. Spaulding from Peterson was instrumental in acquiring the property for the park, which was dedicated in 1934. Civilian Conservation Corps Company 778 built the shelter

evidence.claim: Its rear and side walls use irregular rubble stone. Across the front, four stone pillars carry vertical timbers supporting the roof's eaves. Openings for a door and window punctuate each side wall; a fireplace and chimney occupy the center of the rear wall.
evidence.quote: The rear and side walls are composed of random rubble stone. There are four stone pillars across the front, and four vertical timbers attached to them that support the eaves of the gable roof. Each side wall has a doorway and window opening. A fireplace and chimney are centered on the rear wall.

evidence.claim: Four stone pillars and vertical timbers support the shelter’s front eaves.
evidence.quote: There are four stone pillars across the front, and four vertical timbers attached to them that support the eaves of the gable roof.

evidence.claim: Linn Grove takes its name from a grove of linden trees near the town site.
evidence.quote: Linn Grove was named for a grove of linden trees near the town site.

evidence.claim: Near this Little Sioux River town, the Chan-Ya-Ta Site contains the remains of a 1,000-year-old village. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: The nearby Chan-Ya-Ta Site contains the remains of a 1000-year-old prehistoric village, and is on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: Across the byway corridor, artifacts from the Mill Creek culture date to around AD 1000. Archaeological sites and the museums in Linn Grove and Peterson document this earlier history.
evidence.quote: History buffs will also find evidence of the area's rich Native American heritage in the archaeological sites near the Byway and in the museums of the quaint country towns of Peterson and Linn Grove. Artifacts from the Mill Creek culture date back to around 1000 AD.

evidence.claim: The center interprets glacial features including kames and kettles, hanging valleys and catsteps, alongside the role of prairie in Iowa’s agricultural heritage.
evidence.quote: Learn about glacial remnants, including kames and kettles, glacial till, hanging valleys and catsteps, all in one place. You’ll also see a restored prairie and learn how prairies were vital to Iowa’s rich agricultural heritage.

evidence.claim: Cemented stone covers the floor, and a small stone basement occupies the northwest corner.
evidence.quote: There is a small stone basement in the northwest corner, and cemented stone covers the floor of the shelter.
